controls.title: List your suppliers and rank them by the risk they carry
controls.description: Every supplier with access to your systems, data or premises, or whose failure would disrupt you, is listed with an owner and a risk rating, and is checked before contract in proportion to that rating. You cannot manage risks from suppliers you have not identified.
guidance: Build the list from purchasing records, contracts and the systems each supplier touches.
Rate each supplier on the data it handles, the access it has and how hard it would be to replace.
Ask high-risk suppliers for evidence such as certifications, recent audit reports or answers to a security questionnaire.
Record the outcome and any conditions before the contract is signed.
For each critical supplier, note how you would switch away and get your data back.

controls.title: Put the protection you expect from suppliers in signed contracts
controls.description: Every protection you expect from a supplier is written into a contract it has signed, so you can enforce it if things go wrong. Promises made in sales meetings or emails are hard to enforce.
guidance: Keep a clause library with a basic set for every supplier and an extra set for those holding sensitive data or admin access.
Set a hard deadline, in hours, for the supplier to tell you of a breach that touches your data.
Keep the power to verify: an audit right, or a yearly independent assurance report you can rely on.
Ban silent handovers: the supplier names its subcontractors and asks before adding one.
Agree up front how your data comes back, in what format, and when it is wiped at their end.

controls.title: Find out what is inside the technology you buy
controls.description: Hidden weaknesses in the parts, libraries and subcontractors behind a product can reach you through a routine update. For technology you depend on, you know what it is built from, how its maker fixes flaws and how long it will be supported.
guidance: Ask makers of software you depend on for a software bill of materials (SBOM) and their target time to fix known flaws.
Make passing your security clauses down to their subcontractors a contract condition, and ask for the subcontractor list.
Buy hardware and software only from the maker or its authorised resellers, and accept only signed updates.
Subscribe to each key vendor's security advisories and assign someone to act on them.
Record vendor end-of-support dates in your asset list and plan replacements a year ahead.

controls.title: Keep checking that key suppliers still protect you after signing
controls.description: A supplier that was safe at signing may not stay that way. High-risk suppliers are re-checked on a schedule, and anything they change that affects your data, such as where it is hosted or who handles it, is assessed before you agree.
guidance: Re-check high-risk suppliers at least yearly, using their service reports, audit reports and incident history.
Use regular meetings with key suppliers to go through incidents, open issues and what they plan next.
Ask to be told before your data moves to a new country or a new handler, and assess the move before agreeing.
Raise contract breaches formally and track the agreed fixes to completion.
Re-rate a supplier when what it does for you, or its own situation, changes.

controls.title: Agree who secures what before your data goes into a cloud service
controls.description: Each cloud service you rely on has a written split of security duties between you and the provider, a hardened configuration and a tested way to get your data out. Many cloud breaches stem from customer-side settings rather than from the provider.
guidance: Keep a list of approved cloud services and give staff a way to request new ones.
For each service, write down who is responsible for accounts, configuration, backups, encryption and logs.
Apply a secure baseline configuration and check it for drift automatically where tools allow.
Check where data is stored and processed, and whether that meets your legal and contract duties.
Document how you would export your data and move to another provider, and test the export.
